humor.name: Humor
humor.definition: An umbrella term covering the stimulus (funny thing), the response (mirth), and the behavior (laughter). Attardo distinguishes these three carefully.
examples: A joke is humorous; laughter is the response to humor; mirth is the emotional experience
key_distinctions: humor ≠ laughter (one is stimulus, other is response)
humor ≠ mirth (one is object, other is experience)

joke.name: Joke
joke.definition: A short humorous text with a punchline. Attardo: 'a text which is humorous and which has a punchline.' The punchline is the 'funny part' that comes last and triggers the humor.
examples: Hedberg one-liner: 'I used to do drugs. I still do, but I used to, too.'

punchline.name: Punchline
punchline.definition: The part of the joke that triggers the humor. Usually at the end. Forces a re-interpretation of the setup. Attardo: the 'funny part' that makes the joke work.
examples: '...because the light was on' (Norm moth joke)

mirth.name: Mirth
mirth.definition: The emotional experience of finding something funny. The subjective feeling that accompanies humor appreciation.
examples: The feeling of amusement when a punchline lands

laughter.name: Laughter
laughter.definition: The behavioral response to humor. Not all humor produces laughter; not all laughter is humor (nervous laughter, social laughter).
examples: Audience laughter after a punchline

meta-humor.name: Meta-humor
meta-humor.definition: Humor about humor itself. Jokes about jokes, comedy about comedy. Attardo notes this is distinct from 'humor about X' — meta-humor's target is the humor mechanism itself.
examples: Louis: 'That's just me saying something terrible because it makes me laugh that it's true'
Stewart Lee critiquing his own joke structure live

verbal-humor.name: Verbal Humor
verbal-humor.definition: Humor that depends on language specifically — wordplay, puns, verbal irony. Distinct from non-verbal humor (slapstick, physical comedy).
examples: Puns, double entendres, wordplay

non-verbal-humor.name: Non-verbal Humor
non-verbal-humor.definition: Humor that does not depend on language — slapstick, physical comedy, visual humor. The GTVH does NOT apply to this.
examples: Keaton's physical comedy, pratfalls

release-theory.name: Release Theory
release-theory.definition: Laughter discharges accumulated nervous energy. Freud: jokes are pressure valves for repressed impulses. Spencer: sudden relief from restraint. Bergson: 'the mechanical encrusted on the living.'
examples: The relief laugh after a tense pause
Nervous laughter after a taboo topic
release-theory.maps_to_our: pause-before-punch: tension buildup → release. The hold-then-snap trajectory.

incongruity-theory.name: Incongruity Theory
incongruity-theory.definition: Humor arises when perception violates expectation. Kant: 'laughter from the sudden transformation of a strained expectation into nothing.' Schopenhauer: mismatch between concept and reality. Morreall: pleasant psychological shift from incongruity to resolution.
examples: Norm's moth: expect pest-control punch, get 'because the light was on'
Setup builds frame A, punch forces frame B
incongruity-theory.maps_to_our: punch surprise, garden_path, semantic_distance, DPV framework

aggression-theory.name: Aggression Theory
aggression-theory.definition: Laughter at others' misfortune — their loss is our gain. Hobbes: 'sudden glory' at others' inferiority. Plato: laughter as attack on others. Gruner: comedy as competitive combat.
examples: Roast comedy: laughing at the target's flaws
Superiority humor: laughing at someone's mistake

bisociation.name: Bisociation
bisociation.definition: Koestler's theory: humor arises from the simultaneous perception of an event in two incompatible frames. The 'aha' moment when both frames coexist is the laugh.
examples: A pun: the same word in two frames simultaneously
Louis's confession: sincere frame + absurd frame coexisting

complementarity-principle.name: Complementarity Principle
complementarity-principle.definition: Attardo's key insight: the three classical theories are NOT competing. They describe different aspects of the same phenomenon — release=incomprehension=aggression are complementary layers, not rival explanations.
examples: A roast joke: aggression (target) + incongruity (surprise) + release (tension) all fire simultaneously
complementarity-principle.maps_to_our: Our multi-layer BV model: violation (incongruity) + benign (release+distance) + social target (aggression)

incongruity.name: Incongruity
incongruity.definition: Divergence from expectations. Broader than 'surprise' — includes semantic, script, and tonal incongruity. Attardo: 'generalized as divergence from expectations.'
examples: Setup builds one reading, punch forces another
properties: necessary but not sufficient for humor
can be semantic, script, or tonal

resolution.name: Resolution
resolution.definition: The process by which the listener re-interprets the setup under the new script activated by the punchline. Attardo distinguishes full vs partial resolution.
examples: The 'aha' moment when the punchline makes sense

full-resolution.name: Full Resolution
full-resolution.definition: The incongruity is completely explained. The listener fully understands why the punchline is funny. Classic setup→punch→reframe structure.
examples: Classic one-liner: setup builds expectation, punch completely re-frames

partial-resolution.name: Partial Resolution
partial-resolution.definition: Some incongruity remains after resolution. This is why absurdism works — the incongruity is NOT fully explained, but the audience finds it funny anyway.
examples: Norm's moth: the 'because the light was on' answer is technically correct but the incongruity of the whole digression remains
Lock's absurdist premises
partial-resolution.key_insight: Partial resolution is why absurdism works — the violation REMAINS, but BV's benign frame makes it funny

foregrounded-incongruity.name: Foregrounded Incongruity
foregrounded-incongruity.definition: The incongruity IS the joke. The audience laughs AT the incongruity itself, not at a resolution. Anti-jokes, absurdism.
examples: Norm's anti-jokes: the humor is that there's no real punchline
Andy Kaufman's anti-comedy

backgrounded-incongruity.name: Backgrounded Incongruity
backgrounded-incongruity.definition: Resolution is smooth, surprise is in the TIMING not the meaning. The audience doesn't notice the incongruity because the delivery makes it feel natural.
examples: Louis's confessions: the content is absurd but the delivery makes it feel sincere
Rock's premises: the observation is true, the escalation is surprising
backgrounded-incongruity.key_insight: Backgrounded incongruity = our BV 'benign frame' doing the work — the delivery makes the violation feel safe

isotopy-disjunction-model.name: Isotopy Disjunction Model (IDM)
isotopy-disjunction-model.definition: Attardo's model for linear joke processing: (1) Setup establishes an 'isotopy' — a semantic field directing interpretation. (2) Punchline disjoins the isotopy — forces a different reading. (3) Resolution is re-interpreting the setup under the new isotopy.
examples: Louis Monopoly: setup isotopy='parenting is hard', punchline disjoins='to handle HER', resolution=re-read as father's inability
isotopy-disjunction-model.maps_to_our: DPV framework: isotopy=prediction model, disjunction=temporal+semantic violation

linear-organization.name: Linear Organization of Jokes
linear-organization.definition: Jokes have a linear structure: setup builds expectation (direction A), punchline redirects (direction B). The redirect MUST use material already in the setup — misdirection, not withholding.
examples: Rock's premise rule: if the audience doesn't understand the premise, nothing works
linear-organization.key_rule: The punch must use material the audience already has. New information = failed joke ('well, you didn't tell me that').
linear-organization.maps_to_our: Our 'shortest path' punch: minimal move to disjoint reading using existing setup material

script.name: Semantic Script
script.definition: A large chunk of semantic information about a situation, object, or event. A 'frame' or 'schema' for understanding a piece of the world. From Raskin's Semantic Script Theory of Humor (SSTH).
examples: The 'restaurant' script: you sit, order, eat, pay
The 'doctor' script: symptoms, examination, diagnosis
key_properties: can be opposed to other scripts

script-opposition-SSTH.name: Script Opposition (SSTH)
script-opposition-SSTH.definition: Raskin's foundational insight: a text is humorous IF (1) two scripts are fully overlapped in some region, AND (2) the two scripts are opposed in another region. The overlap makes the joke possible; the opposition makes it funny.
examples: 'The light was on': moth-to-podiatrist script overlaps with moth-to-flame script in the punchline
script-opposition-SSTH.maps_to_our: double_interpret operator (two readings), split_knowledge (audience knows both scripts)

script-overlap.name: Script Overlap
script-overlap.definition: The region where two scripts share elements. The overlap makes the joke POSSIBLE — the audience can move between scripts because they share territory.
examples: Moth joke: both scripts involve a moth, a person, and a destination

script-opposition-opposition.name: Script Opposition (the opposition)
script-opposition-opposition.definition: The region where two scripts conflict. The opposition makes the joke FUNNY — the audience laughs at the collision between incompatible readings.
examples: Moth joke: pest-control destination vs light-attracted destination

GTVH.name: General Theory of Verbal Humor
GTVH.definition: Attardo & Raskin's formal theory: every verbal joke is characterized by 6 Knowledge Resources (SO, LM, SI, TA, NS, LA). Extends SSTH from short jokes to long humorous texts.
GTVH.formula: joke = {SO, LM, SI, TA, NS, LA}
GTVH.key_insight: The 6 KRs are independent — changing any one produces a different joke. This is why our operators work: each changes one or more KRs.

KR-SO.name: Knowledge Resource: Script Opposition
KR-SO.definition: Two semantic scripts that overlap but oppose. The foundational KR — the 'what' of the joke.

KR-LM.name: Knowledge Resource: Logical Mechanism
KR-LM.definition: The reasoning that connects SO to the punchline. The 'how' of the joke. 12 mechanisms identified.

KR-SI.name: Knowledge Resource: Situation
KR-SI.definition: The contextual setting — location, participants, objects, activities. The 'where and who' of the joke.

KR-TA.name: Knowledge Resource: Target
KR-TA.definition: Who or what the joke is about. Can be self, other, group, or abstract concept. Affects the safety math of the joke.

KR-NS.name: Knowledge Resource: Narrative Strategy
KR-NS.definition: How the joke is told — rhetorical structure, pace, rhythm, direct/indirect discourse. The 'when and how' of the joke.

KR-LA.name: Knowledge Resource: Language
KR-LA.definition: The specific words chosen — vocabulary, syntax, sound. The 'surface' of the joke. The most 'free' KR — same joke, different words.
KR-LA.key_insight: LA is the most free KR — the same joke can be told in many words. But words matter for rhythm and emphasis.

jab-line.name: Jab Line
jab-line.definition: A humorous trigger WITHIN the body of a text (not at the end). Attardo (2001) distinguished jab lines from punch lines — long bits have many jab lines, not just one punch.
examples: Tags are jab lines: secondary laughs within the bit
Asides, callbacks, secondary punches
jab-line.maps_to_our: Tags = jab lines. Our 'diminishing returns' on tags is Attardo's jab line economy.

performance-of-humor.name: Performance of Humor
performance-of-humor.definition: Humor is not just TEXT — it's PERFORMANCE. The same text delivered differently produces different results. Performance includes prosody, timing, gesture, audience interaction.

prosody.name: Prosody
prosody.definition: The melody of speech — intonation, stress, rhythm, voice quality. Attardo discusses how prosody carries humor: pitch changes mark incongruity, stress highlights key words, voice quality signals frame shifts.
examples: Louis: quiet envelope (19.6dB) with wide pitch (6.83 st) inside
Carlin: body-in-rhythm-with-voice

timing-performance.name: Timing (Performance)
timing-performance.definition: Where silences fall relative to punchlines, how fast the comedian talks, when to resume after laughter. Attardo: punchlines preceded by substantial pauses (0.6s+). Norrick: punchlines delivered FASTER than setup.
examples: Louis 1.67s average pause (above pro 1.39s)
Norm 192wpm never-stop delivery
timing-performance.maps_to_our: H1 (14x baseline pause), H3 (HOLD then SNAP)

gesture-performance.name: Gesture in Humor
gesture-performance.definition: Body language as part of humor performance. Gestures can create incongruity (body contradicts words), physical timing (Carlin: body-in-rhythm), visual punchlines (Keaton, Chaplin).
examples: Carlin: crouching on setup, standing on punch
Keaton's deadpan physicality
gesture-performance.maps_to_our: PHYSICALITY-AXIS.md (voice-first vs mixed vs physical-first), TIC-TALK kinetic energy r=-0.75

audience-co-performer.name: Audience as Co-Performer
audience-co-performer.definition: The audience is not passive. Laughter SHAPES the performance. Comedians adjust timing based on audience reaction. The feedback loop is essential.
examples: TAMS: audience impacts microtiming
Lock: panel format gives 6 people to do the leg work
'Stay in the bit' (Seinfeld to Louis)
audience-co-performer.maps_to_our: TAMS finding (audience impacts microtiming), panel-show safety net

competence-performance-distinction.name: Competence vs Performance
competence-performance-distinction.definition: Competence = knowing what's funny (text-level knowledge). Performance = making it funny in the moment (delivery-level skill). A joke can have good competence but bad performance, and vice versa.
examples: A well-structured joke delivered poorly = good competence, bad performance
An improvised riff that kills = good performance, unknown competence
competence-performance-distinction.maps_to_our: Our gates check TEXT (competence); delivery/timing topics cover PERFORMANCE

humor-signal.name: Humor Signal
humor-signal.definition: A signal that tells the audience 'this is meant to be funny.' Includes: prosodic cues (exaggerated intonation), framing ('joke's on you'), contextual cues (comedy club setting), and meta-linguistic markers.
examples: The comedian's exaggerated tone signals 'this is a joke'
The comedy club setting signals 'expect humor'
humor-signal.maps_to_our: sincerity doctrine (the character never signals; the PERFORMER signals)

code.name: Code (Semiotics)
code.definition: The system of signs that both speaker and listener share. Humor requires a shared code — the audience must understand the same sign system as the comedian.
examples: Cultural references (UK panel show humor requires knowing the format)
In-jokes require shared knowledge
code.maps_to_our: split_knowledge (shared code the persona pretends not to have)

relevance-theory-humor.name: Relevance Theory and Humor
relevance-theory-humor.definition: Sperber & Wilson's relevance theory applied to humor: jokes work by creating optimal relevance — the audience works to derive meaning, and the effort is rewarded with humor.
examples: The setup creates an expectation of relevance; the punch re-directs it
relevance-theory-humor.key_insight: The audience's effort to resolve the incongruity IS part of the pleasure

context-humor.name: Context and Humor
context-humor.definition: Humor is context-dependent. The same text can be funny in one context and not in another. Context includes: physical setting, social relationship, cultural background, conversational history.
examples: A joke about death is funny at a roast, not at a funeral
UK panel show humor requires knowing the format
context-humor.maps_to_our: jokegate license check (context determines if the violation is benign)

pun.name: Pun
pun.definition: A joke that exploits multiple meanings of a word or similar-sounding words. Attardo: the simplest verbal humor — one word, two scripts.
examples: 'Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana'
pun.gtvh_mapping: SO = two meanings of same word; LM = ambiguity resolution

verbal-irony.name: Verbal Irony
verbal-irony.definition: Saying the opposite of what you mean, expecting the audience to recognize the inversion. Attardo distinguishes from sarcasm: irony is playful, sarcasm is aggressive.
examples: 'Oh, WONDERFUL' when something goes wrong
Lock's deadpan delivery of absurd claims
verbal-irony.maps_to_our: double_interpret (two readings), split_knowledge (audience knows the true meaning)

sarcasm.name: Sarcasm
sarcasm.definition: Aggressive irony. Saying the opposite of what you mean WITH hostile intent. Distinct from verbal irony: sarcasm attacks, irony plays.
examples: Roast comedy is largely sarcasm
'Nice job' said to someone who failed

adjacency-pair.name: Adjacency Pair
adjacency-pair.definition: A pair of conversational turns that belong together (question-answer, greeting-greeting, complaint-apology). Humor often exploits the second slot — the expected response is replaced with a funny one.
examples: 'How are you?' → 'I'm fine, said no one ever'
The punchline replaces the expected second slot
adjacency-pair.maps_to_our: garden_path (setup creates adjacency expectation, punch violates it)

preference-organization.name: Preference Organization
preference-organization.definition: Some conversational responses are 'preferred' (expected, socially marked) and some are 'dispreferred' (unexpected, socially unmarked). Humor often comes from dispreferred responses.
examples: A compliment → dispreferred response: 'I know, right?' (instead of 'thank you')
preference-organization.maps_to_our: garden_path (preferred response = the setup; dispreferred = the punch)

footing.name: Footing
footing.definition: Goffman's concept: the alignment a speaker takes toward their own words. A comedian can shift footing — speaking as themselves, as a character, as a narrator. The shifts create humor.
examples: Louis shifting from narrator to confessor
Acaster shifting from fictional cop to real self
footing.maps_to_our: persona oscillation, modulator_range, unreliable narrator variants

power-solidarity.name: Power and Solidarity
power-solidarity.definition: Humor encodes power relationships. Poking fun UP (at the powerful) is safer than poking fun DOWN (at the vulnerable). In-group humor builds solidarity; out-group humor can exclude.
examples: Roast: mutual poking = solidarity
Late-night monologue: poking the powerful = safe

operationalization.name: Operationalization
operationalization.definition: The process of turning abstract humor concepts into measurable variables. Attardo argues humor studies needs operationalization to be scientific — 'funny' must become countable.
examples: Turning 'incongruity' into 'semantic_distance = 1 - cosine(setup_embed, punch_embed)'
Turning 'timing' into 'pause_duration in seconds'
operationalization.maps_to_our: Our entire measured-timing pipeline: pauses, wpm, syllable counts — we operationalized Attardo's call

corpus-methodology.name: Corpus Methodology
corpus-methodology.definition: Building and analyzing collections of jokes for systematic study. Attardo discusses corpus size, annotation schemes, and the need for representative samples.
examples: Our 34,551 annotated bits from 36 comics
Our 2,373 R2-linked clips with transcripts
corpus-methodology.maps_to_our: characters2 bits_theory.json (34k bits), funnygraph clips_substrate (6,876 clips)

level-of-analysis.name: Level of Analysis
level-of-analysis.definition: Attardo distinguishes levels at which humor can be studied: text-level (the joke structure), performance-level (the delivery), reception-level (the audience response). Different theories operate at different levels.
examples: GTVH = text-level. Timing research = performance-level. Laugh density = reception-level.
level-of-analysis.maps_to_our: Our gates check text-level; delivery/timing topics cover performance-level; laugh data covers reception-level

narrative-humor.name: Narrative Humor
narrative-humor.definition: Humor in long-form narrative — comic novels, humorous stories. Unlike jokes, narrative humor unfolds over time. Attardo discusses how GTVH applies to longer texts via jab lines.
examples: Twain's Huckleberry Finn
Wodehouse's Jeeves stories
Louis's storytelling bits
narrative-humor.key_insight: Long texts have jab lines (within-body humor), not just punchlines (end-triggered)

comic-character.name: Comic Character
comic-character.definition: A character whose traits create humor through inconsistency, excess, or rigidity. Attardo links to Bergson: the comic character is 'the mechanical encrusted on the living.'
examples: Bergson's rigid character
Locke's grounded-absurd persona
Acaster's over-committed idiot

untranslatability.name: Untranslatability
untranslatability.definition: Some humor cannot be translated because it depends on language-specific features (puns, wordplay, cultural references). Attardo argues translation is a test of what's 'essential' in humor.
examples: Puns rarely translate (word-specific)
Cultural references need adaptation
untranslatability.key_insight: What survives translation = the SO + LM (structure). What doesn't = LA (specific words). This confirms the KR independence.

kr-independence-evidence.name: KR Independence (from translation)
kr-independence-evidence.definition: Translation proves the 6 KRs are independent: you can preserve SO+LM+SI+TA+NS while changing LA. The joke still works with different words — confirming LA is the most 'free' KR.
examples: A joke translated to French: same SO, same LM, different LA — still funny
kr-independence-evidence.maps_to_our: Why our operators work: each changes one KR without breaking others

humor-pedagogy.name: Humor as Pedagogy
humor-pedagogy.definition: Using humor in teaching. Attardo discusses how understanding humor mechanics helps in education — both teaching ABOUT humor and using humor TO teach.
examples: Teaching joke structure as a writing exercise
Using humor to make material memorable
humor-pedagogy.maps_to_our: Our series videos ARE humor pedagogy — teaching the mechanics through examples

complementarity-synthesis.name: Complementarity Synthesis
complementarity-synthesis.definition: Attardo's final position: humor studies needs all levels (retrieval, comprehension, appreciation), all theories (release, incongruity, aggression), and all KRs (SO, LM, SI, TA, NS, LA). No single framework captures everything.
examples: Our multi-layer BV model mirrors this: violation + benign + social target
complementarity-synthesis.maps_to_our: Our entire system: gates (comprehension) + delivery/timing (performance) + laugh data (appreciation)

future-directions.name: Future Directions
future-directions.definition: Attardo calls for: more corpus work, better operationalization, cross-cultural studies, computational models. We are literally doing what he called for.
examples: Our 34k-bit corpus IS the corpus work
Our measured timing IS the operationalization
Our UK/US region data IS the cross-cultural study
future-directions.maps_to_our: We are Attardo's future directions, executed

saussurean-sign.name: Saussurean Sign
saussurean-sign.definition: The sign as the indissoluble unity of signified (concept) and signifier (sound-image). A word's meaning is not 'in' the word — it's in the relationship between the signifier and the concept it points to.
examples: 'Bat' signifier → two signifieds (animal vs sports equipment) = the pun mechanism
Literalize: signifier stays, signified shifts to physical meaning
saussurean-sign.key_insight: Puns work because ONE signifier points to TWO signifieds. The punchline selects the second signified.
saussurean-sign.maps_to_our: double_interpret (two readings of same signifier), literalize (signified shifts to literal)

meta-communicative-signal.name: Meta-communicative Signal
meta-communicative-signal.definition: A signal that frames an utterance as 'not to be taken literally.' Bateson's 'play frame': 'this is play' signals that suspend normal meaning rules. In humor: the comedian signals 'this is a joke' via prosody, setting, or explicit markers.
examples: Exaggerated intonation = 'this is funny'
Comedy club setting = 'expect humor'
'Just kidding' = explicit meta-communicative signal
meta-communicative-signal.key_insight: The sincerity doctrine REMOVES meta-communicative signals from the CHARACTER — the character never signals 'this is a joke.' The PERFORMER signals; the character doesn't.
meta-communicative-signal.maps_to_our: sincerity doctrine (character never breaks 4th wall), humor-signal node (expanded)

grices-maxims.name: Grice's Maxims
grices-maxims.definition: The cooperative principle: conversational participants follow four maxims. (1) Quantity: be as informative as required. (2) Quality: be truthful. (3) Relation: be relevant. (4) Manner: be clear. Humor often VIOLATES one or more maxims while maintaining the appearance of cooperation.
examples: Understatement violates Quantity (too little info)
Non sequitur violates Relation (irrelevant)
Pun violates Manner (ambiguous on purpose)
grices-maxims.key_insight: Humor works by APPEARING to follow maxims while actually violating them. The audience detects the violation and laughs.
grices-maxims.maps_to_our: garden_path (appears to follow relation, actually violates it), linear-organization rule

implicature.name: Implicature
implicature.definition: What is implied but not said. Grice's key concept: meaning can be conveyed by violating maxims, because the listener infers the intended meaning from the violation itself. The punchline's meaning often lives in implicature, not in the literal words.
examples: 'Nice job' after failure → implicature: sarcasm (violates Quality)
Louis's confession: literal words are absurd, implicature is sincere fear
implicature.key_insight: The punchline's MEANING is often in the implicature, not the literal text. This is why partial-resolution works — the implicature carries what the literal doesn't.
implicature.maps_to_our: split_knowledge (audience reads the implicature; persona pretends the literal), BV (violation is literal, benign is implicature)

cognitive-effect-effort.name: Cognitive Effect vs Processing Effort
cognitive-effect-effort.definition: Relevance theory: an utterance is relevant when it yields cognitive effects (new implications) for minimal processing effort. Humor is maximally relevant when it yields high effect (amusement, insight) for low effort (easy to resolve).
examples: A clean punchline: high effect (big laugh), low effort (instant resolution)
An obscure reference: low effect (confusion), high effort (can't resolve)
cognitive-effect-effort.key_insight: The best jokes maximize the RATIO, not just the effect. This is why 'simple but surprising' beats 'complex and clever.'
cognitive-effect-effort.maps_to_our: punch length r=-0.32 (shorter punch = funnier = lower effort for same effect), economy score

ambiguity-taxonomy.name: Ambiguity Taxonomy
ambiguity-taxonomy.definition: Three types of linguistic ambiguity that generate humor: (1) Lexical: one word, multiple meanings (polysemy, homonymy). (2) Structural: one sentence, multiple parse trees (garden path sentences). (3) Phonological: one sound sequence, multiple transcriptions (near-homophones).
examples: Lexical: 'bat' (animal/equipment)
Structural: 'Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana'
Phonological: 'I used to do drugs' → 'I still do, but I used to, too'
ambiguity-taxonomy.key_insight: Each ambiguity type is a different SO mechanism. Lexical = two signifieds. Structural = two parse trees. Phonological = two transcriptions. All three are double_interpret at different linguistic levels.

malapropism.name: Malapropism
malapropism.definition: Using a wrong word that sounds similar to the intended word, creating humor through the confusion. Named after Mrs. Malaprop in Sheridan's 'The Rivals.' A specific type of phonological ambiguity.
examples: 'He's the pineapple of politeness' (pinnacle)
Comedians who deliberately use wrong words for effect

tautology-humor.name: Tautology (as humor)
tautology-humor.definition: A statement that is humorously redundant — saying the same thing twice in a way that reveals something unexpected. 'War is war' or 'a deal's a deal.' The tautology violates Grice's Quantity maxim (too little new information) while asserting something the listener didn't expect to be asserted.
examples: 'Boys will be boys' (tautology that reveals expectation)
'It is what it is' used as a comic deflection
tautology-humor.maps_to_our: rigidify (following the identity rule past its usefulness)

repair-sequence.name: Repair Sequence
repair-sequence.definition: When conversation breaks down and gets fixed — misunderstanding, self-correction, clarification. Attardo notes people laugh during failed repair sequences. Comedy often exploits the repair: the breakdown IS the joke.
examples: Comedian misunderstands a heckler on purpose
'Wait, what? No, I said...' — the repair IS the bit
repair-sequence.maps_to_our: garden_path (the breakdown is the violation), crowd work topics

conversation-opening-closing.name: Conversation Openings and Closings
conversation-opening-closing.definition: Conventions for starting and ending conversations. Humor often exploits these: the greeting is the setup, the farewell is the button. Standup openings/closings mirror conversation openings/closings.
examples: 'How are you?' → 'Fine' (preferred) vs 'Let me tell you...' (unpreferred = comedy opening)
'That's my time' = the comedy closing convention

participation-framework.name: Participation Framework
participation-framework.definition: Goffman's framework for who is speaking to whom in an utterance: animator (the voice), author (the words), principal (the beliefs). In comedy, these can be SEPARATED: the comedian (animator) speaks as a character (principal) who didn't write the words (author).
examples: Louis as animator speaks as 'Louis the persona' (principal) — the real Louis's beliefs leak through
Acaster as animator speaks as Springleaf (principal) — real feelings leak
participation-framework.key_insight: The unreliable narrator works because animator ≠ principal. The comedian's voice carries the character's words, and the real person's beliefs leak through the gap.
participation-framework.maps_to_our: persona footing (animator ≠ principal), unreliable narrator variants, split_knowledge

politeness-theory.name: Politeness Theory
politeness-theory.definition: Brown & Levinson: face-threatening acts (FTAs) threaten the listener's positive face (desire to be liked) or negative face (desire to be free). Humor is aFTA that is mitigated — the joke threatens face but the humor frame makes it acceptable.
examples: A roast joke is an FTA mitigated by the humor frame
Self-deprecation is an FTA on oneself (always safe)
politeness-theory.key_insight: THE-LINE IS POLITENESS THEORY: crossing the line = the FTA is too threatening for the humor frame to mitigate. License = stronger mitigation.
politeness-theory.maps_to_our: THE-LINE crossing formula, jokegate license check, edge scoring

gender-humor.name: Gender and Humor
gender-humor.definition: Variationist sociolinguistics of humor: men and women use humor differently. Research shows: men tend toward aggressive/superiority humor; women tend toward affiliative/self-deprecating humor. Attardo notes this is about PATTERNS, not absolutes.
examples: Roast comedy (traditionally male-dominated) uses aggressive humor
Confessional comedy (traditionally more female) uses affiliative humor
gender-humor.key_insight: Gender patterns in humor map to our target types: aggressive→powerful/victim, affiliative→self. Not deterministic, but real patterns.
gender-humor.maps_to_our: target types (self vs powerful), status dynamics

literary-humor-taxonomy.name: Literary Humor Taxonomy
literary-humor-taxonomy.definition: Attardo lists the genres of literary humor: comedy, satire, irony, fantasy, parody, picaresque, farce. Each has subtypes. The taxonomy maps loosely to our comedy formats.
examples: Satire = roast (attacking the powerful)
Parody = meta-comedy (imitating a genre)
Farce = absurdist escalation
Picaresque = story format

unreliable-narrator-literature.name: Unreliable Narrator (Literature)
unreliable-narrator-literature.definition: A narrator whose credibility is compromised — the reader knows the narrator's version is wrong. In literature: first-person narrators who are blind to their own situation. This is the DIRECT literary ancestor of our unreliable-narrator comedy device.
examples: Acaster's undercover cop: the narrator claims to be a cop, the audience knows he's not
Lee's Carpet Remnant World: the narrator claims to have a plan, the audience sees it collapsing
unreliable-narrator-literature.key_insight: In literature, the unreliable narrator creates dramatic irony (reader knows more than narrator). In comedy, it creates split_knowledge (audience knows more than persona). SAME MECHANISM, different medium.
unreliable-narrator-literature.maps_to_our: UNRELIABLE-NARRATOR.md (5 variants), split_knowledge, the entire frame topic

domestication-foreignization.name: Domestication vs Foreignization
domestication-foreignization.definition: Two translation strategies. Domestication: adapt the humor to the target culture (change cultural references). Foreignization: preserve the source culture (keep references, accept some loss). Attardo uses this to show what's 'essential' in humor.
examples: Domestication: change a UK joke's reference to a US equivalent
Foreignization: keep the UK reference, translate only the words
domestication-foreignization.key_insight: What survives domestication = SO + LM + SI + TA + NS (structure). What's lost = LA (specific words) + cultural SI. This is KR independence in action.
domestication-foreignization.maps_to_our: KR independence evidence, region data (UK vs US humor patterns)
